danish.title: Ellevte bog (1812) — Kapitel 8
paragraphs: Henimod slutningen af slaget ved Borodino løb Pierre for anden gang ned fra Rajevskijs batteri, banede sig vej gennem en kløft til Knjazkovo med en flok soldater, nåede forbindingspladsen, og da han så blod og hørte skrig og stønnen, skyndte han sig videre, stadig indviklet i soldaterskarerne.

Det eneste, han nu ønskede af hele sin sjæl, var at komme hurtigt væk fra de forfærdelige indtryk, han havde levet med den dag, og vende tilbage til livets almindelige betingelser og sove roligt i en seng i sit eget værelse. Han følte, at kun under livets almindelige betingelser ville han kunne forstå sig selv og alt det, han havde set og følt. Men sådanne almindelige livsbetingelser var ingen steder at finde.

Skønt granater og kugler ikke peb over den vej, han gik ad, var der stadig på alle sider det samme som på slagmarken. Der var stadig de samme lidende, udmattede og undertiden underligt ligegyldige ansigter, det samme blod, de samme soldaterkapper, de samme lyde af skud, der skønt fjerne nu stadig vakte rædsel, og desuden den dårlige luft og støvet.
Da Pierre havde gået et par mil ad Mosjajsk-vejen, satte han sig ved vejkanten.

Tusmørket var faldet på, og kanonernes torden døde hen. Pierre lå længe lænet på sin albue og stirrede på de skygger, der gled forbi ham i mørket. Han indbildte sig hele tiden, at en kanonkugle kom flyvende mod ham med en forfærdelig hvislen, og så gisp han og satte sig op. Han anede ikke, hvor længe han havde ligget der. Midt om natten satte tre soldater, der havde hentet brænde, sig i nærheden af ham og begyndte at tænde et bål.

Soldaterne, der kastede skæve blikke til Pierre, fik ilden til at brænde og stillede en jerngryde på den, hvori de brækkede noget tørt brød og kom lidt fedt i. Den behagelige duft af fedtede retter blandede sig med røgens lugt. Pierre satte sig op og sukkede. De tre soldater spiste og talte indbyrdes uden at tage notits af ham.

»Og hvem er I så?« spurgte en af dem pludselig Pierre, idet han åbenbart mente det, Pierre selv havde i tankerne, nemlig: »Hvis du vil have noget at spise, giver vi dig noget, bare lad os vide, om du er en ærlig mand.«

»Jeg, jeg...« sagde Pierre, idet han følte det nødvendigt at nedtone sin sociale stilling så meget som muligt for at være nærmere soldaterne og bedre forstået af dem. »Strengt taget er jeg militsofficer, men mine folk er ikke her. Jeg kom til slaget og har mistet dem.«
»Nå, se!« sagde en af soldaterne.
En anden rystede på hovedet.
»Vil I have lidt grød?« spurgte den første soldat og rakte Pierre en træske, efter at have slikket den ren.

Pierre satte sig ved ilden og begyndte at spise grøden, som de kaldte maden i gryden, og han syntes, det var det mest lækre måltid, han nogensinde havde smagt. Som han sad bøjet grådigt over den og tog den ene store skefuld efter den anden og tyggede, blev hans ansigt belyst af ilden, og soldaterne kiggede tavst på ham.
»Hvor skal du hen? Fortæl os det!« sagde en af dem.
»Til Mosjajsk.«
»Er I en herre, ikke?«
»Ja.«
»Og hvad hedder I?«
»Peter Kirilytj.«
»Nå, så kom med os, Peter Kirilytj, vi bringer jer derhen.«
I det fuldstændige mørke gik soldaterne med Pierre mod Mosjajsk.

Da de nærmede sig Mosjajsk og begyndte at gå op ad den stejle bakke ind i byen, galede hanerne allerede. Pierre gik videre med soldaterne og glemte helt, at hans kro lå nede ved foden af bakken, og at han allerede var gået forbi den. Han ville ikke så snart have husket det, så fortumlet var han, hvis ikke han halvvejs oppe ad bakken var stødt på sin staldkarl, der havde været inde i byen for at lede efter ham og var på vej tilbage til kroen. Staldkarlen genkendte Pierre i mørket på hans hvide hat.
»Deres Excellence!« sagde han. »Vi var allerede ved at opgive håbet! Hvordan kan det være, at De er til fods? Og hvor er De på vej hen?«
»Nå, ja!« sagde Pierre.
Soldaterne standsede.
»Så har du fundet dine folk?« sagde en af dem. »Nå, farvel, Peter Kirilytj — var det ikke det?«
»Farvel, Peter Kirilytj!« hørte Pierre de andre stemmer gentage.
»Farvel!« sagde han og vendte sig med sin staldkarl mod kroen.
»Jeg burde give dem noget!« tænkte han og greb i lommen. »Nej, hellere lade være!« sagde en anden, indre stemme.
Der var ikke et værelse at få på kroen, de var alle optaget. Pierre gik ud i gården og trak kappen over hovedet, lagde sig i sin vogn og sov.

english.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 8
paragraphs: Toward the end of the Battle of Borodino, Pierre — having run down from Raevsky's battery a second time — made his way through a gully to Knyazkovo with a crowd of soldiers, reached the dressing station, and seeing blood and hearing cries and groans, hurried on, still caught up in the stream of soldiers.

The one thing he now wanted with his whole soul was to get away quickly from the terrible experiences of that day and return to ordinary life — to sleep peacefully in a room, in his own bed. He felt that only under normal conditions would he be able to make sense of himself and everything he had seen and felt. But such normal conditions were nowhere to be found.

Though shells and bullets no longer whistled over the road he was traveling, on all sides there was the same thing as on the battlefield — the same suffering, exhausted, and sometimes strangely indifferent faces, the same blood, the same soldiers' overcoats, the same sounds of firing that, though distant now, still inspired terror — and in addition the foul air and the dust.
After walking a couple of miles along the Mozhaysk road, Pierre sat down by the roadside.

Dusk had fallen and the roar of guns died away. Pierre lay propped on his elbow for a long time, watching the shadows pass him in the darkness. He kept imagining a cannonball flying toward him with a terrifying whistle — then he would shudder and sit up. He had no idea how long he'd been there. In the middle of the night, three soldiers who had gathered firewood settled near him and began lighting a fire.

The soldiers, casting sideways glances at Pierre, got the fire going and set an iron pot on it, into which they broke some dried bread and added a little fat. The pleasant smell of greasy food mixed with the scent of smoke. Pierre sat up and sighed. The three soldiers were eating and talking among themselves, paying him no attention.

"And who might you be?" one of them suddenly asked Pierre, clearly meaning what Pierre himself had been thinking — namely: "If you want to eat, we'll give you some food, only let us know whether you're an honest man."

"I... I'm..." said Pierre, feeling it necessary to minimize his social standing so as to be closer to the soldiers and better understood by them. "Technically I'm a militia officer, but my men aren't here. I came to the battle and got separated from them."
"Well, well!" said one of the soldiers.
Another shook his head.
"Would you like a little mash?" the first soldier asked, handing Pierre a wooden spoon after licking it clean.

Pierre sat down by the fire and began eating the mash — as they called the food in the pot — and thought it was the most delicious thing he had ever tasted. As he bent greedily over it, scooping up large spoonfuls one after another, his face was lit by the firelight and the soldiers watched him in silence.
"Where do you need to go? Tell us!" said one of them.
"To Mozhaysk."
"You're a gentleman, aren't you?"
"Yes."
"And what's your name?"
"Peter Kirilych."
"Well then, Peter Kirilych, come along with us — we'll get you there."
In the total darkness the soldiers walked with Pierre to Mozhaysk.

By the time they neared Mozhaysk and began climbing the steep hill into town, the roosters were already crowing. Pierre walked on with the soldiers, completely forgetting that his inn was at the bottom of the hill and that he'd already passed it. He wouldn't have remembered this at all, so deep was his state of abstraction, had he not stumbled halfway up the hill upon his groom, who had been looking for him in town and was heading back to the inn. The groom recognized Pierre in the darkness by his white hat.
"Your excellency!" he said. "We were starting to despair! How is it you're on foot? And where are you going?"
"Oh, yes!" said Pierre.
The soldiers stopped.
"So you've found your people?" said one of them. "Well, goodbye, Peter Kirilych — isn't it?"
"Goodbye, Peter Kirilych!" Pierre heard the other voices repeat.
"Goodbye!" he said, and turned with his groom toward the inn.
"I ought to give them something!" he thought, reaching into his pocket. "No, better not," said another, inner voice.
There was no room to be had at the inn — they were all occupied. Pierre went out into the yard and, covering himself from head to toe, lay down in his carriage.
